title: Adaptive learning of density ratios in RKHS
authors: Werner Zellinger, Stefan Kindermann, Sergei V. Pereverzyev
text:
## 1.1 Problem

Let P and Q be two probability measures on a measurable space (\mathcal{X},\mathcal{A}) with compact \mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} and \sigma -algebra \mathcal{A} of its measurable subsets. Assume that P is absolutely continuous with respect to Q. Then, the Radon-Nikodým theorem grants us a Q -integrable function \beta:\mathcal{X}\to[0,\infty) satisfying, for any U\in\mathcal{A},

If both measures, P and Q, have densities with respect to another reference measure, e.g., the Lebesgue measure, then \beta equals the ratio of their densities.

The problem of learning \beta from samples {\bf x}:=(x_{i})_{i=1}^{m} and {\bf x}^{\prime}:=(x_{i}^{\prime})_{i=1}^{n}, drawn independently and identically (i.i.d.) from P and Q, respectively, plays a central role in statistics and machine learning [1]; its applications include anomaly detection [2,3], two-sample testing [4,5], divergence estimation [6,7], covariate shift adaptation [8,9,10], generative modeling [11], conditional density estimation [12], and classification from positive and unlabeled data [13]. Note, that this problem is different from supervised learning [14] as the given data do not include point evaluations \beta(x) from the desired target \beta.

It has been first observed by [15] that many algorithms for density ratio estimation compute finite-sample approximations of the objective \beta by discretizing the minimization problem

where g(f) is a model of the Radon-Nikodým derivative \beta with f\in\mathcal{H} in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) \mathcal{H}, B_{F}(\beta,\widetilde{\beta}):=F(\beta)-F(\widetilde{\beta})-\nabla F(\widetilde{\beta})[\beta-\widetilde{\beta}] is a Bregman divergence generated by some convex functional F:L^{1}(Q)\to\mathbb{R}, \left\lVert.\right\rVert is a norm on \mathcal{H}, and \lambda\in\mathbb{R} is a regularization parameter; see Example 1. For the exact form of the finite-sample approximations applied in practice, we ask the reader for patience until Eq. (11) is stated.

- • As can be seen from [15], the kernel unconstrained least-squares importance fitting procedure (KuLSIF) in [16] uses Eq. (2) with F(h)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}(h(x)-1)^{2}/2\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}Q(x) and g=\mathrm{id}, where \mathrm{id}(f)=f is the identity (cf. [17]). This leads to a discretization of the minimization problem

- • The logistic regression approach (LR) employed in [18] can be obtained from Eq. (2) using F(h)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}h(x)\log(h(x))-(1+h(x))\log(1+h(x))\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}Q(x) and g(f)=e^{f} with f(x)=\theta^{\text{T}}\varphi(x) for some \varphi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}; see [15].

- • The exponential function approach (Exp) introduced in [19] can be obtained using F(h)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}h(x)^{-3/2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}Q(x) and g(f)=e^{2f}; see [19].

- • The square loss (SQ) is used in [19] with F(h)=\int_{X}1/(2h(x)+2)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}Q(x) and g(f)=\frac{-1+2f}{2-2f}.

To the best of our knowledge, no error bounds are known for estimating Eq. (2) for the functionals in Example 1 that take into account the regularity of the density ratio \beta, except [9] and [20] which hold only for KuLSIF. Moreover, except for KuLSIF, no method for choosing the regularization parameter \lambda in Eq. (2) is known that adapts to the regularity of \beta, i.e., a method with error bounds provably decreasing for increasing regularity.

## 1.2 Results

Following [19], one can relate the minimization of the data fidelity term B(f):=B_{F}(\beta,g(f)) from Eq. (2), to the minimization of the expected loss with a loss function \ell:\{-1,1\}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} measuring by \ell(-1,f(x)) and \ell(1,f(x)), respectively, the error of a classifier f(x) which predicts whether x is drawn from P or Q.

Our first result (Example 6) shows that all loss functions \ell corresponding to Example 1, satisfy a property called generalized self-concordance [21]. This allows us to extend results from supervised learning in RKHSs to density ratio estimation.

Our second result (Proposition 2) provides, in a well specified setting, for large enough sample sizes and with high probability, an error bound

for a minimizer f_{{\bf x},{\bf x}^{\prime}}^{\lambda} of the empirical estimation Eq. (11) of Eq. (2) with appropriately chosen regularization parameter \lambda. The regularity index r and the capacity index \alpha in Eq. (4) originate from source conditions as used in inverse problems and learning theory. In the special case of square loss (SQ), the error rate in Eq. (4) is minimax optimal in the same sense as it is minimax optimal in supervised learning, see [22,23].

Our third result (Eq. (30)) is a new method for choosing the regularization parameter \lambda that does not need access to the regularity index r but nevertheless achieves the same rate as in Eq. (4) (see Theorem 2). Our method is based on a Lepskii-type principle balancing bias and variance terms of a local quadratic approximation of the (generally not quadratic) data fidelity B(f). Our parameter choice strategy achieves the error rate in Eq. (4) and is thus optimal in the case of square loss. A numerical example illustrates our theoretical findings.

## 1.3 Related Work

The representation of density ratio estimation methods as minimizers of empirical estimations of Eq. (2) has been first observed by [15] and later characterized in more detail by [19]. Our work extends [15,19] by taking into account the effect of the regularization term \frac{\lambda}{2}\left\lVert f\right\rVert^{2} in Eq. (2).

In general, to the best of our knowledge, there are no error bounds similar to Eq. (4) for the class of discretized minimization problems Eq. (2). For the special case of KuLSIF in Eq. (3), error rates have been discovered in [17,9,20]. In particular, the error rate discovered in [17], for RKHS with bracketing entropy \gamma\in(0,2), is

This rate is worse than the one in Eq. (4), whenever \alpha(2r+1)>\frac{2}{\gamma}. A similar result for KuLSIF and the special case of Gaussian kernel, is presented in [24], see Type I setting there. We can also mention [9] which provides the error bound

with r^{\prime} originating from a source condition similar to our Assumption 5 but for the covariance operator T=\int_{\mathcal{X}}k(z,\cdot)\otimes k(z,\cdot)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}Q(z) of Q instead of \rho, where k denotes the kernel of \mathcal{H} and (u\otimes v)[f]=\langle u,f\rangle v the rank- 1 operator. Our result in Eq. (4) improves Eq. (6) for \alpha\in(1,\infty) and 0<r^{\prime}\leq r\leq\frac{1}{2}. In the recent work [20], Eq. (6) is improved by additionally taking into account the capacity of the space \mathcal{H} in terms of a new pointwise source condition on the reproducing kernel of \mathcal{H} that allows to bound the regularized Christoffel function. Such condition can be used as alternative for the effective dimension as defined in our Assumption 6. As a result, an error bound similar to our Eq. (4) is obtained in [20]. However, the error is measured in the \mathcal{H} -norm and the bound holds only for the special case of the KuLSIF.

To the best of our knowledge, the balancing principle introduced in this work is the first parameter choice method for density ratio estimation with discovered error rate. We can mention variants of cross-validation [17], the quasi-optimality criterion [20], and hints towards the use of balancing principles [9], but, even in the special case of KuLSIF, we are not aware of any finite-sample error bounds related to these approaches.

Some of our proof techniques rely on [21], where self-concordant loss functions in the context of kernel learning were studied first. Our analysis extends [21] to density ratio estimation and adaptive parameter choice.
